speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the years, technological advancements and market and societal changes have significantly affected how works and performances are created, distributed and consumed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for example, new and more accessible technologies have democratised content creation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Now, anyone can be a photographer or even produce a short video or film.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: New platforms enable these new creators to reach their audiences directly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Faster Internet speeds have shifted consumption from physical media and downloads to streaming and the ubiquity of smartphones has led to consumption on the go.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And a public consultation on the draft Bill was held in early 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We received over 500 responses from both individuals and organisations alike.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We heard from various stakeholders in our copyright ecosystem who shared with us their views, perspectives and also their interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are the rights owners, the consumers, from the industry, academics and also legal practitioners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Bill, which is the culmination of the review, responds to these changes and prepares us for what lies ahead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To aid in understanding which provisions in the Bill relate to the provisions in the current Copyright Act, with your permission, Mr Speaker, may I ask the Clerks to distribute an annexure to the Members?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members can also access these materials through the SG PARL MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members will see that this annexure cross-references each provision in the Bill to its corresponding provision in the current Copyright Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As you can see, the organisational changes are quite extensive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members may also notice that quite a few provisions in the Bill in the annexure that you now have before you do not have a corresponding provision in the current Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first category of changes will benefit creators and rights owners to reward them for their creations and also enable them to create new works.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Anyone who uses authorial works or protected performances in public must identify the author or performer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The specific circumstances in which identification must be given depends on the work or performance in question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a person must identify the author of an artistic work like a photograph whenever the person publishes it, such as in a book or perhaps in corporate materials, or communicates a visual image of it, such as sharing it online or on a social media platform.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill also provides for exceptions where identification is not needed, including if the identity of the author or performer is not reasonably ascertainable by the user, in computer programs or when the work is an artistic work situated in a public place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Parties can continue to use contractual arrangements to manage their obligations to identify the author or performer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, where the author or performer waives his or her rights in writing, then he or she does not need to be referred to or identified.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The attribution rights as a creator are personal to the author or performer and cannot be assigned to a third party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As this new right is separate from the economic rights relating to copyright, users must still identify the author or performer even if they have a licence to do the relevant acts comprised in copyright, such as a licence to publish the work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in cases where the author or performer and the rights owner are not the same person, it will be necessary to obtain permission from both parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This right to be identified is only enforceable by civil means via injunctions and damages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 385(2) provides that the Court must consider all relevant matters in deciding on the appropriate remedy, including the defendant's awareness of the author or performer's right to be identified or anything done by the defendant to mitigate the effects of the infringement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, creators of commissioned works like illustrations or text for corporate collaterals have default ownership of their works.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, creators of other commissioned works, in particular, photographs, portraits, engravings, sound recordings and films, do not have default ownership.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In those cases, it is the commissioning party that owns the copyright by default.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This change therefore aligns the default position so that there will be no difference amongst the different types of commissioned works.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a photographer hired to take photos at an event would by default own the copyright to those photos he or she took.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While parties can continue to use contractual arrangements to adjust copyright ownership, this puts our creators in a better position before negotiations with the commissioning party commences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They also had difficulty in utilising the existing provisions in the Copyright Act to enforce against the sellers of such devices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We reviewed the situation and concluded that new liability provisions tailor-made for these situations and, taking into account future use cases, would be useful and would also provide clarity for the industry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus, while the predominant issue today is with devices which facilitate access to films and cable programmes, the new provisions will also be broad enough to cover other types of content like books and songs and other methods such as offering of services to install apps on existing hardware.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The change targets people who commercially profit off hardware, software and services which have only a limited commercially significant purpose or use and other than to facilitate access to copyright works communicated to the public without the authority of the copyright owners.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Acts of a commercial nature, such as commercial dealings by way of sale, offering for sale, distribution for the purposes of trade, will fall within the scope of the new provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new provisions are technologically neutral: it applies equally to acts in a brick-and-mortar setting as they do to acts on the online platform.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a liability is imposed on a retailer, whether in a physical shop or online, who knowingly sells a set-top box or other devices containing pre-loaded applications that provide access to streaming sites housing pirated content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These new provisions provide copyright owners with specific remedies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They should utilise these provisions when enforcing their rights against commercial dealings in these devices, apps or services instead of other liability provisions in the Bill that copyright owners may have previously sought to rely on in the past, in the absence of these specific remedies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In tandem with the introduction of these specific remedies, we continue to encourage content owners to provide a broad selection of affordable, high-quality content to consumers to attract them onto such platforms with legitimate content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also want to urge consumers to respect intellectual property (IP) and consume legal offerings so that we can incentivise creators to produce more quality content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second category of changes will increase the scope of permitted use of works and protected performances to benefit society at large and I will turn to this now.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, let me highlight the change which helps in the use of works and recordings of protected performances for education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The use of Internet materials for educational activities has increased in importance over the years and now, even more so, particularly in the context of the pandemic, with home-based learning and other online activities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is limited to Internet materials that are generally accessible to the public for free.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a teacher can include news articles or blog posts that are freely accessible on the Internet in lesson plans or homework assignments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The student, in turn, can use these materials for their projects or their assignments in school.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One condition is that the teacher or student must not knowingly use Internet materials which infringe copyright.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If they unknowingly do so and subsequently receive a notification from the rights owner, then, they must stop using the material.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the material has been communicated to the public, they must take reasonable steps to prevent further access to the material.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any further use of that material would not be allowed under this permitted use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The limitation of this permitted use of free Internet materials allows our teachers and students to source from many different up-to-date sources without adversely affecting the incomes of the educational publishers who can continue to charge for their offerings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another set of beneficiaries are the print-disabled, for example, the visually impaired, or those who cannot manipulate physical hardcopy books.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2014, we passed certain provisions relating to the Marrakesh Treaty, a treaty concluded under the auspices of the World Intellectual Property Organization or WIPO, which seeks to facilitate access to copyright works for persons with print disabilities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have since received feedback from the users of these provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, the requirement to pay fees to rights owners when organisations help people with print disabilities convert works and protected performances into accessible formats was seen as making the conversion process even more expensive and time-consuming.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also effectively charged persons with print disabilities twice, since they would have already purchased a copy of the work or the recording of the performance for the organisation to make the conversion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The change supports the needs of the print-disabled community and Singapore's commitment to building a more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This also continues to be in line with Singapore's international obligations under the Marrakesh Treaty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To give Members an example, this permitted use can be relied on when training an Artificial Intelligence programme or using computers to analyse large databases of materials, without needing to seek permission from each rights owner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will apply in both commercial and non-commercial contexts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, the user must have lawfully accessed the relevant materials, for example, he or she should not have accessed the materials by circumventing a paywall.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This supports our Smart Nation initiatives, our push towards data-driven innovation and Singapore's efforts to grow our Artificial Intelligence and technology sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At this juncture, Sir, let me highlight that I would also be moving two amendments to the Bill at its Committee stage, to correct a drafting omission in clauses 247 and 248.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These clauses allow the use of sound recordings and recordings of performances under specified circumstances, subject to payment of equitable remuneration to the copyright owner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments, Sir, replace the term "copyright owner" with the term, "rights owner" in both clauses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The latter is a broader term and also includes persons who are entitled to bring an action for infringing uses of a performance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the scope of the exception covers performances, the amendments ensure that there is a corresponding obligation to pay the rights owner of the performance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: CMOs are private organisations that represent groups of rights owners to grant licences to users.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is an efficient way for users to get licences from a large group of rights owners.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, users often get licences from CMOs to play songs in public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The alternative would be for users to have to seek permission directly from the composer and the lyricist of each song.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the years, we have had feedback from both rights owners and users regarding the behaviour of certain CMOs who, for example, refuse to give information on their repertoire or how they distribute royalties among their members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In response, an arrangement was reached in 2012 for CMOs to self-regulate through a voluntary code of conduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, since then, for a variety of different reasons, the CMOs have ceased to apply this code of conduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our public consultation in 2017 garnered feedback that the earlier concerns still remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus, the need for some oversight of CMOs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will not control the prices that the CMOs charge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this regard, the Copyright Tribunals will continue to hear any disputes over questions surrounding the reasonableness of licence fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are also safeguards to ensure the proper exercise of such powers, including the right of a CMO to appeal to the Minister in cases involving more severe penalties, such as where a CMO is ordered to cease its business.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill will also rationalise and update the existing criminal offences relating to works and protected performances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Part 8 of the Bill provides for these offences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The penalties reflect the severity of the different types of criminal activities and will more effectively deter future acts of infringement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We had made three key changes in this respect.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the structure has been redesigned, overhauled, to improve the organisation of the legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, we have taken the opportunity to ensure that the Bill is written in plain English, for ease of reading and understanding.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For existing provisions that have been rewritten in plain English, section 9B of the Interpretation Act helps to clarify that such changes in style do not affect the meaning just because different forms of words have been used to express the same idea.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, we have included illustrations showing how certain provisions should be applied in common situations to help rights owners and users understand their rights and obligations more easily.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, clause 204, which permits the use of freely accessible Internet materials for educational purposes, contains illustrations that will help teachers understand the scope of such permitted use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because copyright affects everyone, whether as a rights owner or user, these changes will make the Bill easier for all to understand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At slightly over 320 pages, the Bill is a significant undertaking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The responses we have received in our various public consultations, including the most recent one for the Bill itself, have been generally supportive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Respondents tell us that the Bill meets its goal of responding to the challenges and opportunities of the current digital environment and also being easier to understand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Importantly, this Bill will play its part in helping Singapore maintain our top-class intellectual property regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although I studied the Copyright Act in 1987, I do not practise Intellectual Property in my practice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In his textbook on The Law of Copyright in Singapore, the author, Prof George Wei explained that the justification for copyright protection was to "protect the fruits of an intellectual's activity, labour and investment from unfair appropriation or unfair competition." In an explanatory note about the Copyright Bill 2021, Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) explained that the changes to be implemented by the Bill ensure that "our copyright regime continues to provide an environment that benefits both creators and users.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It introduces new rights and remedies to provide more recognition for creators to further incentivise the creation of works.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It also creates new exceptions for users, allowing copyright works to remain reasonably available for the benefit of society." Sir, I support the principles behind the Copyright Bill 2021.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is only fair that a creator of works who had put in great effort either to write a book, to write or record a song, to perform a dramatic or musical or literary work or to produce a computer game or software program, he should be able to benefit commercially for his or her intellectual efforts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I recall many years ago that a person can easily buy pirated cassettes of songs sold at pasar malam at a fraction of the actual costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: You can find entire books being photocopied wholesale and students using these photocopied books in class.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even when I started working, there are computer sales staff who would offer to load pirated word processing software onto the desktop computer that I bought.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Pirated computer games are often copied and sold openly in some shops.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Such breach of copyright is not correct because it takes away all the efforts of the authors who had written the books, the songs or the software.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It discourages creative work of authors and unfairly allows those who infringe copyright to profit without putting in their effort.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Copyright Bill 2021 is a comprehensive Bill of some 348 pages.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I support the Bill but I wish to seek clarifications on some of the changes to the existing Act which MinLaw had highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is a slightly different position from the current section 30(5) of the Copyright Act whereby the ownership of the copyright of the artistic works would belong to the person who engages or commissions the author for valuable consideration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As an illustration, in a case where a consumer engages a photographer to take a video or photographs for a wedding or a birthday party or a family function, he may not be aware that the position has changed and that he need to expressly sign a written agreement to retain ownership of the copyright of his photos or the video.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Without the written agreement, the photographer or the videographer may be able to retain these personal photographs of the consumer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Government to embark on an education exercise to inform consumers as to the changes which may impact their lives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe many individuals may not be comfortable that the photographer, whom they engage to take photos for their wedding, birthday, or social function is entitled to keep these photos in his portfolio.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If they are paying the photographer or the videographer, why are they not the owner of the copyright?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I support the strengthening of the Fair Use exceptions contained at clauses 190 to 194 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although the concept of copyright is to protect the intellectual outputs of the creator of the works, the Government needs to balance the rights of the IP owner versus the public interest involved or the needs of society to use the works for education or research or certain other purposes as described in those clauses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Ms Ng-Loy Wee Loon, the author of the textbook, Law of Intellectual Property of Singapore, quoted Sir Isaac Newton as saying, "If I have seen further, it is by standing on ye shoulders of giants".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is a reminder that every IP creator is building on works created by those who come before him.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, the law should allow for the use of certain types of copyright because it would advance the interest of the public.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is also clear that some creators of current copyright works today are only able to do so because there were other foundational creative works done by people before them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This clause allows schools and students of non-profit educational institutions to use certain works or recordings or performances available on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If these private schools have to pay for the royalties, it is likely that they will pass on the additional costs of copyright fees to their students who are also consumers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I know of many Singaporeans who are mature students and pursuing their further education in commercial education institutions, which are for-profit.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, I wish to talk about commercial dealing in set-top boxes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I understand that this clause 150 refers to the sale of set-top boxes which allows the buyer of the set-top box to gain access to various online audio or visual content.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I can appreciate how this clause is intended to stamp out the sale of set-top boxes in some shopping complexes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But the reality is that similar set-top boxes are also easily available in other countries and in particular, just across the Causeway.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, it would be a loophole where consumers cannot buy infringing set-top boxes in Singapore but can do so easily overseas.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, a consumer, who is a video producer, who wishes to use a song for his home-made video as background music, would need to find out which is the CMO which can issue him a licence for the use of the lyrics or the song in the video.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He has to enquire whether the CMO is the only organisation allowed to collect the royalty.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He then has to negotiate the fee collected by the organisation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, individuals and commercial entities that play or broadcast music in their restaurants, hotels, malls, offices or shops would be able to deal with the correct CMO and negotiate for the payment of the royalty in a transparent manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will begin by stating my support for the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I will point out a number of residual concerns that I have, notably, on the duration of copyrights, copyrights associated with sound recordings, default ownership of copyright works and fair use provisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will conclude by taking a step back and asking the broader question of whether intellectual property law has fulfilled its intended purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To the good, it streamlines the expiry of copyrights to a common 70 years, starting either posthumously or from the date of creation or publication, depending on the nature of the work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such harmonisation and simplification, in general, are certainly welcome in the areas of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inherent in this simplification, however, are a number of implicit choices that, to my mind, raise some questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Limiting the duration of copyright for anonymous works to 70 years is certainly better than perpetuity, which was the case before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But setting aside minimum terms stipulated in international conventions, why would such a long duration of protection be necessary in the first place?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With no identified author, who would be the beneficiaries of a 70-year copyright and more importantly, would conferring such protection generate net benefits for society rather than releasing its use to the public domain?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I shall return to this more general point about the benefits and costs of granting intellectual monopolies at the end of my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Again, while I understand why such consistency between clauses may be attractive, we should be aware that this inhibits the free usage of such works for the purposes of teaching and research, which yield benefits of their own instead of extending additional rent to copyright beneficiaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I move on, I would just add that while the comparatively longer copyright duration of 70 years is certainly the norm in most high-income countries, this is by no means unanimous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Canada, Hong Kong and New Zealand have also chosen the lower threshold of life, plus 50 years instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it is worth noting that the minimum term in the Universal Copyright Convention is a mere 25 years while Berne Convention's stipulations are either 25 or 50 years, depending on the nature of the work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would Ministry share how this 70-year duration then was chosen?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I should point out that there are consequences to both affording copyright for sound recordings as well as taking EU intellectual property standards as a benchmark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One concern of sound recordings has to do with a practice that is a foundation of modern hip-hop music sampling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This applies especially to drum brakes and modify soundscapes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is now a large body of precedent cases that have resolved on either side of infringement of fair use, but the point I wish to make here is more general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By admitting sound recordings into copyright protection, we run the risk of shutting down whole genres of emergent creative output.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The pertinent question then, is whether the fair use provisions outlined in Part 5 are sufficient to preclude such overzealous applications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Has the Ministry considered how such potential instances of abuse may in fact be managed?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More of a strict adherence to EU standards for intellectual property may end up being a slippery slope.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Members of this House will be aware of the stringency of EU geographical indications and traditional specialties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is the reason why we cannot, even if we had the skills, know-how and wherewithal to, produce Camembert or Scotch Whisky.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken to the extreme, even suggestive terms such as "Parmesan-style cheese" would be prohibited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While these protections almost always apply to agricultural products and hence are largely of academic interest in the Singapore context, we should not be so dismissive of unintended concessions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has recently embraced artisan beer and spirit manufacture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And there is a risk that stipulate designations such as whiskey with an "e", Ouzo or Grappa cannot be applied to the work of our own craft producers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, on the other hand, clause 134 defaults ownership of copyright for sound recordings and films to employers, so long as the work was produced over the course of employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could argue that clause 134 is simply an extension of the current position to cover other types of works and one could further contend that these are two distinct circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the former, the author is a contractor performing a one-off service and hence, would retain the rights to their creations; while in the latter, the employees engage in a regular employment contract and hence, is being fully compensated for the energies in producing works on behalf of the employer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, Mr Speaker, this is an artificial distinction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In both cases, there is payment for services rendered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An employment contract is simply a series of extended one-off commissions and payment for regular employment is paid in lump sum form during payday as opposed to the end of each commission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whether the rights to a creation resides with the author or the employer should, therefore, be a matter of private negotiation between the two parties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There seems to me to be no reason why the law should necessarily confer copyright to one party versus the other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To see this, it is simply sufficient to observe, for example, that photographers routinely offer package deals where the client may either purchase all images and the associated rights or they may pay a nominal amount for a set of printed images, without the rights, to the images or their soft copies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a result, the two sets of clauses come across as self-contradictory, at least from a logical point of view.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This preserves the transparency of the process while ensuring that the weaker party in the employment relationship, typically the employee, holds the initial bargaining power for their intellectual creations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a routine consumer and producer of intellectual property (IP), I regard Part 5 governing fair use provisions as central to the business of ideas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is truly where the rubber hits the road.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Permitting usage of IP is crucial not just from an educational perspective, which is dear to my heart as a teacher, but as any researcher will tell you, an entire intellectual edifice stands on the shoulders of earlier discoveries and developments, as Member Lim Biow Chuan has pointed out before me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Set against this is the need to avoid abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One only needs to be reminded of the American painter and photographer Richard Prince's notorious appropriation art and the risk that an excessively permissive regime may discourage innovation altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, the limitations defined in the Bill, as they stand, remain unclear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But five pages may simultaneously be too much and yet too little.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Five percent of a volume of collected works or five pages of an integrative scientific periodicals such as Science or Nature may well encompass entire articles, whereas five pages of an involved mathematical article may not even include all the pages of a single proof.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that many exemptions of the Bill are for learning purposes in educational institutions, the text is still unclear if this applies uniformly to research exercises as well and whether such use will remain acceptable in a non-educational, but knowledge-based non-profit such as a privately registered think-tank or research institute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, school-based plays often do charge to cover overheads and possibly raise funds, but are, nevertheless, non-profit in the sense that student actors and backstage crew are unpaid amateurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fair use provisions also raise an important meta-question that has plagued academic publishing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All these examples underscore the potential for copyright to be abused and circumvented, even when fair use provisions are carefully crafted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such rent-seeking undermines the scholarly enterprise, which relies on the free exchange of information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, it is generally better to err on the side of permissiveness, insofar as educational endeavours are concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Has the Government considered advancing similar legislation here?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to close with a somewhat more philosophical reflection on the entire presumption that intellectual property rights are a necessary extension of physical property rights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The conventional case claims that, since transmission of ideas is free, we must, therefore, confer on them protective rights, because the failure to do so would lead to a collapse in incentives necessary to support innovation and invention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ideas are, ultimately, embedded in knowledge which, as anyone in this House who has slaved over textbooks will know, must be acquired at a cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By the same token, the ability to develop and embed these self-same ideas into profitable goods and services – the "development" part of R&D – requires a non-trivial and certainly, non-free, amount of human capital to effect the required transformation and a similar costly process of embedding said knowledge into economically-valuable physical capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, just because the technical specifications for, say, the latest microchip, may be freely available, it does not mean that you or I will be able to launch the next Intel or Motorola.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We still need to hire engineers who are, indisputably, not going to work for free, to be able to realise the final product.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And there is no guarantee they will do a good job either.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, economic research has shown that innovation could still occur under competitive conditions, even in the absence of IP rights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would occur if technological improvements enable the quick recovery of sunk costs from the market, for example, when digital-rights management tools can be applied to restrict unabashed replication of books and music, even without the threat of legal force, or when a growing economy reduces the need for intellectual property protection, because growth itself can generate sufficient short-term rents that more than compensate for the opportunity costs incurred in innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The case does, admittedly, become more complicated when we extend our mental model to include not just a home country, but also a foreign one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, protecting foreign IP may even turn out to encourage domestic innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, when targeting IP at goods produced in poorer countries may well raise the innovation rate, the converse would result if IP were directed and targeted at rich-country goods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Far be it that I should be perceived as suggesting that we should go ahead and eliminate intellectual property rights and withdraw from the World Intellectual Property Organization.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a move would be, to say the least, extreme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, my contention is simply that as much as intellectual monopolies may provide incentives for innovation, they may also encourage socially-costly rent-seeking behaviour, and we should be aware of this inherent trade-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this speech, I have provided a number of examples of potential abuse and overreach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, the only way such overreach may be contained is to ensure that those called upon to resolve contending claims remain sensitive to these trade-offs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I should point out that this is only the case if there are mechanisms in place to ensure that those adjudicating these cases possess the capacity to evaluate potentially highly technical presentations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The risk, so amply demonstrated in the United States' patenting system, is that highly paid attorneys and technical specialists run rings around time and knowledge-constrained public officers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In closing, Members of this House who listen to Taylor Swift’s music may be aware that she recently sought to re-record many of her earlier songs, initially released under the Big Machine Records label, which still holds the copyright to those original recordings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the need for Tay Tay to re-record her own music was to recover control over what she believed to have been a blatant abuse by the record company of the extant IP regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This episode is a reminder to us that, at some point, even the biggest megastars were once obscure and subject to exploitation by unscrupulous industry insiders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The amendments will cement and continue to strengthen Singapore’s world-class IP regime.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, it will also provide enhanced protection to creators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The rapid technological advancements accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic have altered the landscape for creatives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, almost anyone and everyone can be both a creator and/or a user of copyrighted materials.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Accordingly, the amendments are a timely move to cater to this changing sphere.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my work in NTUC and the Labour Movement, I have had the opportunity to interact closely with various associations, freelancers and creatives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the past years including recently, NTUC has organised face-to-face sessions with them to better understand, empathise and assist with ground issues and concerns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Apart from ground engagement with freelancers, we also hold regular legal primers under our LawWorks collaboration with the Law Society Pro Bono Services Office and have been doing so since eight years ago.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These legal talks are aimed at distilling and providing solutions to legal issues faced by freelancers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Just two months ago, we conducted a legal primer titled "Freelancing in the New Normal" which addressed, amongst others, common IP questions they had.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Recurrent questions include whether they own the rights to the virtual content produced, how contractual clauses may alter the position and how they may best protect their rights.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I recall vividly some seven years ago when NTUC arranged an engagement cum dialogue session between the Professional Photographers Association of Singapore and the Minister for Law at NTUC Centre.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The freelance photographers raised PDPA issues and challenges with PDPC, and which were eventually resolved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The issue of creator’s rights also came up at that dialogue then, and the freelancers and us in the Labour Movement lobbied for a change in the Copyright Act to better protect creator’s IP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With today's amendments, I would like to express my appreciation to the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) and MinLaw for developing this set of legislative amendments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is a product of countless consultation sessions over the past years between NTUC, the Government and our freelancers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Like they say, the journey of a thousand miles begins with one step.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Having achieved some success in this lobbying front, we are spurred and encouraged to do more.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We remain deeply committed towards improving the lives and livelihoods of our freelancers and freelance professionals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Moving on to the details of the Bill, I will focus on two key changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I applaud the amendments, as they augur well for the creators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With a plethora of content easily available and accessible to all, proper attribution of work will ensure creators are duly recognised for their creative work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Apart from spurring creativity within the community, creators would also be in a better position to commercialise their works for future assignments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This serves to level the playing field, in part, considering that service buyers, such as multinationals and companies, usually have an edge over individual freelancers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Should the service buyers wish to own the IP rights, they would have to negotiate with the creators for the same, which would typically involve a higher payment in exchange for the assignment of IP rights.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While the Bill is no doubt commendable, I would like to highlight the existing challenges that freelancers face in the realm of contract negotiations and IP rights.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, the lack of bargaining power in negotiations with service buyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The changes will benefit creatives; there is no question about that.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, the reality remains that there exists a power asymmetry between the creators and freelancers as individuals and companies as service buyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A common gripe amongst creators is that service buyers adopt a "take it or leave it approach".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As a result, they are unable to meaningfully negotiate without being seen as difficult, for fear that the work will be awarded to someone who is more compliant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In other situations, service buyers may drive a hard bargain, forcing creators to accept lower fees for their services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The power asymmetry between parties is particularly acute in Government contracts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, if the Government requires freelancers to make an unlimited number of revisions to the product, they will have less time and energy for other projects.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Correspondingly, this would mean less income for them too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This problem is exacerbated by freelancers bearing all upfront costs associated with procurement of all materials and expenses required for the project.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead, Government employees are instructed to use such content or material prepared by the freelancers, for cost-saving purposes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Quite apart from the onerous contractual obligations that freelancers must shoulder, a culture of fear is also perpetuated by various agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Freelancers are concerned that these onerous clauses are being replicated across multiple agencies and tenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As these onerous terms are seen as the "norm" within many of these Government contracts, freelancers face significant resistance each time they attempt negotiations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If they broach this issue, there is a real fear that they will be "blacklisted" for future Government tenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There may be practical difficulties associated with enforcing the right of attribution, especially if multiple parties refuse to attribute the creator.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some may be deterred from instituting proceedings for a breach, due to prohibitive legal costs and difficulties navigating the legal system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This problem may be further exacerbated in situations where users of the works are located outside of Singapore, which presents extra-territorial jurisdictional issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to ensure that any legal recourse available is accessible, affordable and expedient in rooting out such unwanted behaviour.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Creativity is a bedrock of inventions and creators the builders of an innovative society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Prior to the pandemic, freelance performers were paid for each of their "live" performances.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Such practices would stifle innovation and creativity, to the detriment of our society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this respect, what more can be done to protect the lives and livelihoods of our freelancers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And to that end, I would like to suggest some solutions for consideration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These solutions may be summarised using what I call the three "Es".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First E, exemplification by the public sector; second E, educating the public, service buyers and freelancers; and the third E, enlightening the service buyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, for the public sector to take the lead to roll out these amendments and observe the changes, in other words, to lead by example.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Where possible, to allow them to retain default ownership over the commissioned works and not have it varied by contract.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Perhaps, a licence could be considered, with the scope of the licence to be negotiated between parties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Otherwise, the intended benefits of the amendments may be nullified.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Where reasonable, to accede to their requests for less onerous contractual terms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For instance, limiting the number of revisions to be made by the freelancer before the project is deemed as "completed" and/or implementing interim payment milestones to ease their financial constraints.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And it is hoped that when the public sector leads by example, the private sector will follow suit too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, we need to do more to educate the public.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In one of my dialogues with a freelance professional, he explained that in the course of his work, he had to obtain various licences and permits from seven different publishing houses to use and perform a particular performance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: He told me that it was an administrative hassle determining who he had to liaise with, especially since each publishing house owned different rights over that single performance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In his words, I quote, "It is not that we do not want to comply, We want to comply, we really do, but we do not know how to!

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is too confusing." In this regard, it is humbly submitted that educating the public on easy and fuss-free methods of compliance with would help Singapore retain its position as an IP hub.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A one-stop publishing house dealing with all the IP rights would also be useful.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Another aspect of education involves educating the service buyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As highlighted earlier, some of these onerous clauses are terms "copied-and-pasted" across many contracts and thus regarded as the "norm".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As some of the service buyers are not legally trained, they are therefore averse to any amendments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Accordingly, a basic course and guide on contract principles may be useful so that once service buyers are aware of their rights and implications, they would be less resistant towards contract negotiations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And where reasonable, they would be inclined to agree to it, which would expedite matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: MinLaw and IPOS may consider producing quick reference guides, infographics and a list of FAQs and/or webinars for creators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Developing a set of precedent clauses for the creatives' use in their contracts with service buyers would certainly be helpful too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And finally, the third E relates to enlightening the service buyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is perhaps the most difficult of the three solutions, as it requires a fundamental paradigm shift on the service buyers' part.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead of viewing creatives as "difficult" to work with, why not view them as partners embarking on a joint project?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead of gunning for the lowest price possible, why not consider the years of experience and expertise which justify their fees?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead of imposing regimental requirements on them with no room for manoeuvring, why not consider flexible arrangements which are mutually beneficial?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our freelancers have taken a great hit in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: All we are asking for is that the Government and other service buyers treat our freelancers fairly, to give them an opportunity at earning a decent keep because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Let us continue to work together for a brighter future for our freelancers and a brighter future for Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The objectives of the Bill are laudable and include upholding Singapore's international obligations relating to intellectual property (IP), updating and rationalising various aspects of our existing laws on IP and improving accessibility to and ease of understanding these laws.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Critically, it also confers upon authors and performers the moral right to be identified and includes provisions governing fair usage of IP matters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is these final two elements of the Bill that I will concentrate my speech on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, on the granting of new rights for creators and performers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We support the recognition of IP in the works of authors and performers, yet, I believe that there is room for us to expand such recognition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In many other jurisdictions, for example, the UK, US, Australia, New Zealand and various European countries, creators and performers earn residual payments, or royalties for the use of their works and performances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, writers and actors of television programmes broadcast by the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) earn royalties.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is in contrast to the situation in Singapore where writers and actors on Mediacorp television programmes do not do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is further notable that creators and performers have organised themselves into guilds and unions, such as the powerful British performers' union "Equity" and the Writers' Guild of Great Britain, which have not only been crucial in fighting for better pay and working conditions for their members, but are also key in protecting such practitioners and their livelihoods in the wake of the devastation wrought by COVID-19, by negotiating with employers to improve working terms and conditions, improve and ensure diversity in their ranks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also have a right to be consulted on various matters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The ability to have such representation and rights recognised was particularly important as the industry was wrecked by the lockdowns and restrictions brought on by the coronavirus and will be key in helping them to weather any future major disruptions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the Screenwriters' Association (Singapore), while doing good work for the training and development of its members, does not have the power to negotiate minimum standards and protections for its members, and is limited to providing feedback to IMDA focus group meetings upon invitation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With this in mind, I would like to ask if the Government intends to go even further to recognise the rights of creators and performers by legislating for them to receive royalty payments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is the change in copyright law, meant to be a step in that direction?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A further question arises about the presumptions that apply for authorial works that are first published in Singapore, as contained in clause 167.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that these assert a territorially-premised copyright claim.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, it is less clear what the protections and provisions available for international and enforcement of such claims are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What cross-border legal resources are available and are these embedded within a new copyright protection regime?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are not abstract and theoretical questions, as recently seen in the case of a dispute that arose earlier this year over one of our beloved National Day songs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, I wish to raise a number of considerations and clarifications relating to the exceptions introduced by the Bill, primarily the change from a "fair dealing" to a "fair use" exception, which form an extensive part of the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Division 2 of the Bill replaces the fair dealings provision in sections 35, 36, 37, 109, 110 and 111 of the existing Act with the concept of fair use, which "depend on the facts", while still being subject to the considerations specified in clause 191.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This shifts the treatment of alleged copyright infringements away from the fair dealings doctrine – the treatment under English law, where violations must fall into categories defined in the statue – toward a more open-ended fair use doctrine, the approach adopted in the US, where factors did not match any exhaustive list.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, the Bill's open-ended fair use exception now means that the Court need to determine whether the fair use exception applies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that this discretion opens up the possibility of significant ambiguity, particularly in the beginning without a body of case law to back it up.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially in the case of online content and for themes that are deliberately ambiguous, such as memes or parody.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could be confusing for existing content creators who might only have guidance to what would constitute "fair use" of their works but undertaking costly and time-consuming litigation over the potential infringement of their ownership rights.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would IPOS provide specific illustrations of when a use connotes fair use versus when it would not?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such an approach would further the Government's purpose for introducing the fair use exception, in particular, to "create an environment conducive to the development of creative works".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One potential way forward would be for industry associations to take the lead and issue guidelines on what "fair use" would look like for that particular industry, an approach that MinLaw appears to have considered, as mentioned in 2019 MinLaw and IPOS Copyright Review report.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on whether industry efforts are currently underway to develop such guidelines?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I do see that this is a helpful and necessary exception to have, particularly in the advent of more and more powerful AI capabilities and Singapore's drive to be a Smart Nation, it remains to be seen in the real world if the safeguards and conditions are sufficient to balance protecting the rights and commercial interests of copyright holders against allowing legitimate use of copyrighted material for text and data mining purposes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While many modern end-users, raised on the steady diet of electronic media, intuitively grasp instances of copyright violations, could the Minister clarify what efforts have been undertaken to educate the public at large on what constitutes a copyright violation, how to attribute copyright owners appropriately and how to avoid infringing copyright?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, copyright provisions apply to all Singaporeans and it would be especially embarrassing and unfair for our citizens, in particular, that uncle who has just discovered the joys of the "forward" function on WhatsApp, to find themselves inadvertently running afoul of the copyright law as a result of sharing content.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I support, in principle, the control of set-top boxes and related services as this assists in the enforcement of the protection of IP rights.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe that we still need to guard against a situation where IP protection results in access programming becoming prohibitively expensive and therefore, no longer accessible to all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It will be unfortunate if the only way in which one could lawfully gain access to content, in particular, sporting events, would be to pay exorbitant amounts in order to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Key to this is knowing why else would many otherwise law-abiding citizens resort to using set-top boxes and services to access their desired content.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is in addition to the special subscription rates that go over and beyond basic sports packages that avid followers of the English Premier League have to pay.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Overshadowing all these is that Singaporeans pay significantly more for such content than those in most other countries, even those with higher costs of living.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would not be the first to point out here that in years past, Singaporeans could watch live broadcasts of any sporting events and certainly, I am old enough to remember the thrill of being allowed to watch the epic Wimbledon Final between Steffi Graf and Martina Navratilova in 1988, which was telecast on free-to-air TV.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Copyright Bill before us today was described by WIPO as Singapore’s biggest copyright reform in 30 years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I, like many Singaporeans, understand the importance of IP protection and would support the authentic versions unequivocally.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, we still need to guard against a bad situation where IP protection inadvertently results in access to media content becoming an expensive luxury.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, it would be unfortunate if the only way in which one could lawfully watch the English Premier League (EPL) is through paying for exorbitant packages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, why would there be so many otherwise law-abiding citizens resorting to using set-top boxes or other relevant services to watch their favourite content?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Take the Euro 2020 football tournament in June for example, to access to all matches, you must pay an exorbitant fee of $90.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And let us not forget EPL fans who have to pay for an expensive sports package subscription fee each month.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Bear in mind that Singaporeans pay more for similar content than those in most other countries, even those with higher cost of living.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Will certain major sporting events be broadcast free-to-air or perhaps be shown at Community Clubs?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will go some way towards preserving access to sports, which has proven to be a great unifier in our otherwise multicultural and multi-ethnic nation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It could also bridge the digital divide for ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would definitely give us all something to talk about over our morning coffee at our neighbourhood coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, we are constantly generating new works and new copyrights at a rate that we may not even be aware of.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Because of its wide-ranging application, it is timely that the Government is seeking to simplify and update the existing Copyright Act and to draft it in plain English to make it easier to understand for the laymen.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: An important aspect of the Bill is the enhanced clarity on the permitted uses of copyright works.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will allow for aggregation and analysis of data for such purposes as sentiment analysis or machine learning.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These, ultimately, have a public interest aspect to synthesise data for better understanding of, for example, social or economic trends.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, this will support the development of technologies in machine learning and deep learning, which, by their very nature, require the input of a voracious volume of data.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The permitted use will allow access to this data without having to seek approval or licensing from each copyright owner, which may be a significant obstacle.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I highlight this, in particular, because digital material is now increasingly utilised in academic work and the existing Act does not adequately deal with what are the permitted or fair uses of such works.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that this will encourage more conversions of works into formats accessible by print-disabled users.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This provision is forward-looking and inclusive and I commend the Government for taking this very specific step in legislating support for the print-disabled members of our society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This default position is now extended to photographs, portraits, engravings, sound recordings and so on.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, where the contract commissioning the particular work is silent on copyright ownership, the creator will own the copyright by default.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is currently taken for granted when commissioning photographs or films, for example, that the commissioner of the works would own the copyright to the works.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This change in position has a very real on-the-ground implication.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In an instance where a couple engages a photographer to take their wedding or pre-wedding photos or videos, they need to ensure that the engagement agreements specifically mention that the copyright would vest in them instead of the photographer or videographer if they wish to own the copyrights.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, they may be in for a rude surprise that they do not even own the rights to their own photographs and may have to pay further sums to have the rights transferred to them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, in this regard, I urge that efforts be made to educate the public of the change of position and what they should do if they wish to own the copyrights to works that they commission.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the Bill will introduce a regulatory framework on collective management organisations (CMOs).

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In MinLaw's report on the public consultation on proposed licensing of CMOs, members of CMOs and users identified several concerns, including, inter alia, the lack of transparency on how CMOs determined the usage of licensed works to calculate the distribution of fees collected.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This has engendered significant suspicion of CMOs by the industry.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, it is timely that the Ministry imposes a regulatory framework to enhance transparency, good governance and accountability in CMOs, which will go a long way in addressing members', users' and indeed, the public's apprehension of how CMOs operate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, with regulation, naturally comes increases in costs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I urge that the Government balances effective regulation with cost control such that increased cost of operation of the CMO is not passed on to creators, in that they receive less royalties for the use of their works.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, they may also need some time to implement internal standard operational procedures (SOPs) for both governance and reporting, given that they were hitherto unregulated.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the Government may wish to consider a gradated approach where regulations kick in over some years so that CMOs are able to cope.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Further, I would also urge that regulations are not so onerous as to be prohibitive for new entrants into the market and should not stifle new, different and potentially more efficient ways of operating a CMO.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While this is a fairly new area of technology and a complex category of intellectual property rights, the Government may wish to start considering legislation that can definitely fix the ownership of AI-generated works.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Copyright Bill is a timely update to ensure that we stay in step with changes in technology, meeting the needs of a growing creative economy and the increased use of data in the form of audio, video and text in all aspects of our lives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Copyright Bill seeks to establish a well-functioning copyright system that will help content to be created and attributed rightly, distributed efficiently and consumed fairly.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to raise some suggestions to ensure that Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) among us have equitable and fair access to consume and enjoy creative copyrighted content.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many PWDs are artistically inclined and are very creative.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Copyright Bill, with provisions for default ownership as well as the right of attribution to be with the creator, will enable creators who are PWDs to have an income from their creation and that their rights are protected.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding this, we need to also ensure that they are given the same level of access to creative works as the abled so that they can enjoy content and be inspired by it.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that the Copyright Bill contains exceptions intended to give persons who are print-disabled greater and more equal access to copyrighted works.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Intellectual and cognitive disabilities cover a wide range of disabilities that affect mental processes of a person.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This includes disabilities, such as Down's syndrome, autism, learning disabilities like dyslexia, brain injuries from illness or trauma and dementia.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They result in difficulty in processing complex information, requiring a transformation of the material into more easily understood forms.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This transformation can include plain and simple language or high/low versions of written and audio works; changes in formatting, including pictorial illustrations and text-to-speech technology, which help people with dyslexia to access print content.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The same considerations that apply to Persons with Print Disabilities should also apply to Persons with Intellectual Disabilities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Converting content into a form accessible by Persons with Intellectual Disabilities would likewise be expensive, time-consuming and would add to the cost incurred by effectively paying twice to consume the work.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will bring the treatment of copyrighted works equal for persons with print or intellectual disabilities and likewise, ensure fair and equitable access for both.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the copyright provisions are for the print-disabled, which include those with visual impairments, perceptual or reading disabilities or physical disabilities that impede the ability to manipulate a book.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, technology has made creative content much more immersive, requiring both audio and visual senses to fully participate and enjoy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Content on the web is a rich visual and audio experience which can include audio-visual recordings, documentaries and video reports.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the hearing impaired to consume such content, it will have to be transcribed into an accessible copy that includes subtitles or sign language.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would ensure that PWDs with different or multiple disabilities will have fair access to content.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, as we seek to be a more inclusive and fair society, we must make every effort for PWDs to freely participate in the cultural life of the community to enjoy the arts and its benefits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important then that this access for PWDs to enjoy works, regardless of the contractual agreements in place between creators and users.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this respect, I would like to propose for consideration that Division 4 and Division 5 of Part 5 to be included in the list of exceptions from being restricted by contracts so that the authorised entities would be able to provide accessible copies for PWDs, beyond those who are print-disabled, without having the heavy burden of verifying the contractual terms or the fear of a breach of contract.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will encourage greater participation and inclusion of PWDs in our growing arts and cultural works.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, this should also be done and carefully applied such that it does not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the creators.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a society, we have grown and matured in our expression and appreciation of arts, culture and creative content.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the Copyright Bill, we are putting in place a framework to acknowledge the rights of creators and value their work, and updating the law for the digital age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to recognise that PWDs can and should be able to access and participate in the cultural, arts and creative expressions like any of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
