text: I hope that MinLaw will consider my suggestions so that we can build a truly inclusive and fair society.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.21 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will touch on three points in my speech.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are for educational purposes, if they acknowledge the source and cite the access date.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During home-based learning, some teachers face challenges with producing compelling learning content for their students.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As the Internet is a gold mine of educational content, it is sensible to tap on it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should come without encumbering teachers with the onerous requirement of getting consent, as long as the content is readily available for use.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Students will, in turn, be reminded to discern the legitimacy of online sources, as well as to reference them in their assignments, when they see their teachers properly quoting their sources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The right to be identified and the mandatory acknowledgement of sources will help to cultivate a culture that recognises creators.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Starting young also helps to inculcate the right habits of referencing and the value of honesty as they progress academically.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Teachers can also inculcate the right referencing styles and the use of reference management programmes, especially as our youth become more tech-savvy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As assignments become more complex, students increasingly use online resources for their projects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such skills will guard against plagiarism and ingrain the right values.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government share on efforts to build up this culture in our schools?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the challenging employment landscape, more young Singaporeans are turning to freelance content creation, with the hope of eventually turning it into a career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The proliferation of e-commerce has led to a surge in demand for digital marketing services and consequently, visual content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The gig economy has provided increased opportunities for graphic designers and content creators to work on projects and earn an income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not only within Singapore, but also from an international market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But to do so reliably, they must be able to defend the intellectual rights to their concepts and creations, as well as to guard against unscrupulous people who may plagiarise their contents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, how can they expect to be fairly renumerated, if their creations and ideas can be copied and used by others without repercussions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without such safeguards, such gig economy content creators may no longer find it worthwhile to create unique content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I know of a young designer who had once pitched a logo design to a company.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Eventually, the company did not engage his services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But when the company revealed their logo design, he found that it bore great resemblance to the design that he had created.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He was convinced they had misappropriated his design and merely altered it slightly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, he thought it would be too troublesome and costly to take legal action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He also lacked confidence in achieving a successful outcome, as he did not copyright his design.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a perpetual challenge for young content creators, especially those who are just starting out, to protect their works from companies preying on their inexperience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, there must be effective and affordable means of enforcement for such matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it is meaningless if creatives are unable to effectively enforce their rights in an affordable manner and to seek recourse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mediation is probably one cost-effective way to deal with such matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having volunteered as a mediator in MinLaw's Community Mediation Centre, I am an advocate for mediation before litigation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have witnessed many disputes due to a misunderstanding or a lack of awareness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many people are intimidated by the idea of Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, mediation is always a more approachable and affordable means for problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) offers mediation as a formal route to settle copyright disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even so, the costs can be hefty for a freelancer just starting out.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That, alone, may exceed the cost of a brand logo design.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The victim may feel that the cost, time and effort to go through mediation are not worthwhile in pursuing the matter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the rise in independent content creation, it is timely to consider a separate mediation route that is more affordable and streamlined.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The goal is to make mediation more accessible to independent gig economy workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides mediation, there should be other mechanisms, such as tribunals and so on, that could be set up to hear such disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is likely to be increasingly widespread due to the borderless nature of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is for the purpose of facilitating public interest.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is reassuring to know that we can simply forward an infographic from the Government's social media accounts to debunk myths, without fear of legal repercussions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many of my Yio Chu Kang residents, especially seniors, do not enjoy reading walls of texts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, simple-to-understand infographics and digital pamphlets from the various Government websites, are very much appreciated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The agencies' logos on the materials save us the trouble from having to determine the legitimacy of the source.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I recalled previously that a grassroots volunteer wanted to produce a community event flyer that would also contain information on social distancing and mask wearing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He was unsure whether it would be legal to copy the contents from the MOH website.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many would promote their creations and portfolios on social media, from music to visual content, source codes and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is timely that we update the copyright laws accordingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As mentioned in my speech, our copyright laws should not merely protect the rights of creatives to commercialise and prevent exploitation of their work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should also respect the work of creatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will encourage more Singaporeans to share their creative works and inspire others, knowing that it is respected and protected by law.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On one hand, placing too many restrictions on the flow of ideas and creative work and society hinders the possibility of good ideas being built upon and turned into great ideas, disallowing society from standing to collectively gain from the brilliance of individuals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the other hand, too few restrictions discourage these individuals' expressions of brilliance, believing they will not stand to gain from their creations, in turn, dealing a fatal blow to the generation of ideas from a society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is why I and the Labour Movement welcome the troubleshooting of the Copyright Act, as the Government endeavours to adapt to changing concerns and the evolving landscape of innovation and creativity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially pertinent to a league of freelancers in our society: the Creatives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Creatives come in all forms, from the visual, to the literary, to the musical, even the culinary and the floral arts!

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most of us would be quick to diagnose that the depressed wages of creative freelancers to the harsh mechanics of the free market.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like very much to raise the visible and sometimes unethical hand involved in contracting practices with our Creatives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we welcome efforts to give first ownership of copyrights to authors and makers in commissioned work, the reality of transactions between Creatives and their clients runs back much further.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even before contracting, Creatives often find themselves having to pitch their work to their clients, who will, in turn, choose who to commission for the job.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the long run, Creatives are subject to a race to the bottom in terms of their compensation because it is not great ideas that are rewarded but, instead, their willingness to forsake a fair wage.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Strong and sensible contracting terms are welcomed, but an inquiry into pre-contractual interactions, such as pitching, must be also considered in this debate.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Creatives often want their work to entertain, inspire, relate, tell a story and there is, indeed, power in their creations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, the power of the creative work is never far detached from the person behind the creative work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As one freelancer expressed, "art is a reproduction of myself".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Any inquiry into the great creative works of yore never find themselves detached from their creators.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Listen to the familiar tune of "Für Elise" and we remark, "ah, Beethoven".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Marvel at the great paintings and we quickly call to mind "Monet" and "Rembrandt".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This very intimacy between the Creative and their creation is what our copyright laws serve to protect.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this sacred bond is well protected when it comes to most creative mediums, an often overlooked demographic of Creatives are those who happen to express their craft visually and through their likeness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At this juncture, I would like to share a story of my resident, Miss Duan, who has recounted her experience to me as a model.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To perfect their craft, Miss Duan tells me how Creatives do not just "sit and look pretty".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They actually chisel out a whole entire lifestyle around their craft.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The preparation for a shot is often extensive, requiring collaboration across photographers, stylists, dieticians and producers, as well as comprehensive planning, including location, dressing, equipment, amongst others.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Modelling is hard work and the often-elegant final product betrays the amount of hard work that has been poured into the process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, our laws must create meaningful forms of transactional safety nets among Creatives who wish to use one another's work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To conclude, in order to safeguard the interests of Creatives in Singapore, we must make considerations that reflect the realities of transactions between freelancers and their clients, and amongst the Creatives themselves.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Accommodations must also be considered for niche creative fields, such as modelling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill to strengthen Singapore’s copyright regime is necessary and timely.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill will be important in encouraging creativity and protecting creators and their works, carving out crucial fair use exceptions and strengthening the copyright ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have three points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the safeguards on the permitted use of materials for text and data mining for analytic purposes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not clear why we have designed such a specific carve-out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why should creators not have the power to protect their works specifically from being the input data for some machine-learning model?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the principle behind this special condition?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should note that the results of computational data analysis may be extremely profitable and it is not necessarily the case that the original creators may know or be comfortable about their work being used in this way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry share how it intends to ensure a balance between allowing the use of works for computational data analysis and the interests of copyright holders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point relates to enforcing the new right of attribution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome this development as it gives creators recognition for their efforts and respects their work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, in practice, independent or smaller creators with limited resources may not easily be able to monitor publications of their works and enforce their rights.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if creators discover a breach of their rights, they have to bring an action in Court under section 383.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In that scenario, the legal costs might be too high to make enforcement worth it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, the available remedies under section 385 include injunctions and damages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It may not be cost-effective for creators to seek injunctions and damages may be difficult to prove and quantify.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if additional measures will be taken to help these creators enforce their rights?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will the Ministry consider creating a special Court process or use the Copyright Tribunal for a cost-effective means of enforcement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point of clarification relates to the expanded rights of creators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support this new default position in the legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These new rights are supposed to give individual freelancers and creators from small- and medium-sized enterprises greater bargaining power to negotiate better terms with commissioning parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These default positions can be restricted and excluded by contract.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The safeguards are that the contract must be individually negotiated and the contract term purporting to restrict the exception must be deemed to be “fair and reasonable”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is often a power imbalance with creators on one end and publishers and producers on the other.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Publishers and producers may use these same rights against creators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Publishers and producers are likely to favour contracting with creators willing to cede copyright ownership rights to them, rather than one who wishes to retain it or negotiate better terms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the Ministry views legislative intervention a blunt tool in addressing these issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also aware that the Ministry instead plans to collaborate with industry associations to develop sector-specific self-help resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, can the Minister clarify if there are additional resources that will be put in place to level the playing field further?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As individual freelancers and small- and medium-sized businesses lack financial resources for litigation in the case contract terms are found unreasonable, what alternative avenues of recourse are available to this group?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: First is the right to be identified; second, on computational analysis; and third, on CMOs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I believe in the right for creators to be properly identified and take credit for work done.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must honour the creative work of our authors and performers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As this will be the foundation to build an ecosystem based on recognition, respect and reputation for our Singapore creatives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is an important step for creators of original content to build their personal reputation and incentivise the creation of new works with more equitable rights.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: On the amendments for computational data analysis, I welcome the change as we step into the world of data analytics and AI.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is relevant in the information age to enable greater freedoms on the use of information for data analysis to spur a deeper understanding of our world and the domain, which would in turn build a more vibrant and responsible data-driven ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides pursuing artistic excellence, financial benefit is another factor that will motivate the copyright holder to produce more good work.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Copyright Bill provides that acts outside Singapore do not infringe the moral rights of creators or performers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Copyright Bill appears to support a measured balance between the public interest in permitting the use of computational data analysis and the legitimate interests of copyright owners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It remains uncertain how the safeguards for copyright owners will be interpreted in light of the growing use of artificial intelligence and machine learning platforms to perform autonomous data mining.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I applaud the idea of attributing the work to the creator.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, in reality, it may be challenging to identify the creator or performer of the performance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If my interpretation is correct, commissioners of works are to ensure appropriate assignments are entered into with the creators.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How about the contracts signed before November 2021?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are the commissioners going to incur legal costs to ratify these contracts?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the new Act grandfather the contracts signed before November 2021?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Copyright holder needs to know that reworking of fair use into an open-ended exception is not a straightforward process as it will require determination by the Courts as to whether the potential infringer can avail itself of the new exception in any given situation on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Until the Courts have decided, infringers are likely to cite new open-ended fair use exception to defend against allegation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Paraphrasing commonly known legal concepts into layman's language can lead to misunderstanding on the part of the public as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the introduction of the term "permitted use" to describe not only legal exceptions to copyright but other "permitted uses".

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It may cause confusion for a common man.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important for the public to understand that the copyright owner is not permitting the use; in fact, in the case of a legal exception or fair use, no concurrence is required.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It may be better to be precise, emphasising that a fair use is a legal exception to a copyright holder’s monopoly right, not one that has been "permitted" as in the case of a licensed use.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fifth factor to determine "fair use" has now been omitted from the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that it is subsumed in the fourth factor, in other words based on the effect of the use on the potential market.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I feel that this is not as straightforward as the previous wording in providing guidance to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Copyright Bill provides people who are print-disabled such as the visually impaired greater access to copyrighted works.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This amendment will further promote an inclusive society in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When talking about an inclusive society, it is difficult to ignore the problem of illegal set-top boxes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their speeches illustrate some of the competing issues that we face when designing this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Having more exceptions and making inroads to free use or widening fair use all mean less recognition for creators, less remuneration that they receive for their works.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Broadly, in four categories as follows: one, some of the difficulties that rights owners might face; second, clarifications on some of the changes; third, they have raised several suggestions for further changes to be considered; and finally, the communication of these changes to the public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will address Members' queries in these four baskets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Patrick Tay highlighted that the change in the default rules of ownership helps to put creators in a better negotiating position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But creators who are freelancers or small business owners might still face the imbalance of negotiating power that can negate the benefit of the change.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we cannot, however, legislate for negotiating power.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill would not be able to take into account the relative considerations in every commercial negotiation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if we legislate that creators will always have ownership, regardless and do not allow contracts to change this position, this might not cater for situations where the creator wants to assign or sell his or her own copyright for good commercial reasons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A good example is NTUC's Freelancers and Self-Employed Unit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It seeded an industry association, the Visual, Audio, Creative Content Professionals Association, or VICPA; worked with Law Society Pro Bono Services to develop and publish a handbook, "Advocate for the Arts: A Legal Handbook for the Creative Industries".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The UK Society of Authors and the Australian Society of Authors similarly support their members in the same fashion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to work with Government agencies overseeing the development of the various industry sectors to encourage and to support the development of industry associations and industry best practices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Encouraging organisations who commission works to act more reasonably is another factor that would help the current situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay had a couple of good suggestions on how the public sector can lead by example and how service buyers can be educated on basic contract principles.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue with our education efforts within the public sector on these procurement issues and also work with Government agencies to explore how we can educate other service buyers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On enforcement, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Shawn Huang highlighted that creators and performers may lack the financial resources to take enforcement action against infringers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng, in particular, asked whether there could be a special court process created or whether the Copyright Tribunal could be a cost-effective means of enforcement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested that there could cheaper alternatives such as mediation for freelance creatives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have received much of this feedback and discussed it a lot with stakeholders during public consultations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A solution would have to stretch beyond the current legislative amendments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will ensure that there are cost-effective enforcement options available and that creatives who are individuals or small business owners will be made aware of them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Its aim is to provide creators and performers a quick and easy way to assess their situation, to decide if they own the copyright, what is the level of infringement, what the next steps might be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Typically, there is a 45-minute session with an IP specialist lawyer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Advice can be sought on any IP infringement issue, including enforcement options.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, many clear situations can be resolved by a simple letter asserting rights, by telling the alleged infringer of the rights and asserting them, and asking that the user then stop their actions, pay the licence fee or, in the appropriate cases, give credit for the application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, we are continuing to make Court processes more accessible to creators and performers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I believe the fees mentioned by Mr Yip Hon Weng are for mediation of copyright disputes in Singapore under the auspices of WIPO's Arbitration and Mediation Centre, or WIPO AMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These fees are in fact the result of IPOS' existing collaboration with WIPO AMC to reduce mediation costs for copyright disputes and are already highly subsidised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, we are already exploring with other Government agencies on how to make mediation even more accessible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Don Wee asked how creators and performers can enforce against people outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Ms He Ting Ru also raised the same point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They protect copyright within the territory, that is, Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the key point is that these are infringements that take place within our jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, other countries have similar copyright regimes which allow rights owners in Singapore to take action against acts of infringement that might occur in their countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several Members had questions on the details of the changes and I will now turn to a few of them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked whether, instead of written agreements, oral agreements can be used to change the default position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Don Wee asked how past contracts are treated with the change in the default ownership for commissioning situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intention here is not to add on a further overlay of disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Consumers typically are even more vulnerable between the two parties if oral agreements are allowed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is often going to be one man's word against another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But having said that, we will consider Mr Lim Biow Chuan's suggestion, which is a good one, for a template for a written agreement of copyright ownership.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ensures that the existing contractual arrangements which have already been entered into will not be affected by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Don Wee had a question on the challenge for users to identify the creator or performer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had mentioned it earlier but let me just reiterate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There will be appropriate exceptions where identification would not be needed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, when the identity of the creator or performer is not reasonably ascertainable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked about the duration for protection and whether these are based on our international obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He might know that we are bound by the United States-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (USSFTA) and the European Union-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (EUSFTA), which have a minimum duration of protection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is what we have provided for in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is higher than what other countries are bound to and this stronger protection of IP is balanced in this case by the various permitted uses in the Act, which I had discussed earlier and which Members had spoken about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also asked about new provisions on sound recordings and whether they are EUSFTA obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They only add new rights related to public performance and broadcasting of sound recordings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It should be noted that we already protect sound recording rights today, for example, to prevent copying.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To our knowledge, based on the extensive feedback and the industry consultation, there is no evidence that this protection, which also exists in other countries, would inhibit creativity in new areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also asked about the change of default ownership and I think he spoke about the employer-employee relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is based on international industry and legislative norms, including what the UK does for their framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was also discussed with stakeholders during our consultations and public consultations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point really is, the Bill sets up a default position from which parties can negotiate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think that is a point Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point is that the position in law, as set out in this Bill, is the starting point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But there has to be a starting position, as a default.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked whether there would be a loophole that consumers can buy from other countries set-top boxes that stream unauthorised sources of content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was done having regard to striking a right balance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prevalence of such devices and services is an issue around the world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Different countries are at different stages of dealing with this issue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Eventually, it is likely that these devices and services will also be banned or legislated against in other countries too.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also asked whether the permitted use in relation to Internet materials for educational purposes for non-profit schools could be used by for-profit schools, charitable organisations or Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs), and if not, whether it could be extended to them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Again, the point I made at the outset is, we strike a balance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The more inroads you create in terms of exceptions or fair use, the less likely it is that creators and content owners will be appropriately remunerated for their content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, here is a balance and we believe that clause 83, which defines educational institutions that can benefit from this permitted use, strikes the right balance, requiring them to be non-profit, generally covering full-time education and also includes training for adults for their profession.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about charitable organisations and IPCs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They can avail themselves of this permitted use if they fall within the criteria of clause 83.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned, this is a balanced position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Copyright owners' interests also need to be considered when we legislate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Around the world, copyright permitted uses for educational purposes only cover non-profit schools in general.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even if for-profit schools, charitable organisations or IPCs cannot avail themselves of this permitted use, there could be other permitted uses or exceptions which might apply, like fair use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I believe Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned what happens in a situation where you want to use the material for non-educational but knowledge-based think tanks, if I heard him correctly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this situation, the fair use does not prescribe restrictions to the type of organisations which might avail themselves of the fair use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On computational data analysis, several Members asked some questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the safeguards for rights owners, particularly in light of the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Shawn Huang asked whether the permitted use would treat rights owners whose work is instrumental to the outcome of the computational data analysis differently, such as requiring attribution or protecting their commercial interests.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Mr Louis Ng asked why it cannot be restricted by contract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think I mentioned that in my initial speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The conditions of permitted uses were developed with that in mind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To answer Mr Shawn Huang, let me explain the principle behind permitted use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In short, because computational data analysis does not itself make use of the expressive nature of the works, the rights owners' reputational and commercial interests are not adversely affected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, some permitted uses are mandatory for public policy reasons because the benefit of that particular permitted use could be drastically reduced or even non-existent if we allow contracts to modify its application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we protect certain categories which are necessary for public policy reasons, and computational data analysis is one such category.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The benefit of data analysis improves as the set of underlying data used is as complete as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It supports the development of useful applications of data analysis, which is indispensable to the current digital economy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, this permitted use only covers materials to which a user must have had lawful access, such as by paying the subscription fee for the database.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, where the creators or publishers of the materials charge fees in order for users to access such works, that revenue would not be affected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether the new permitted use that allows for dissemination of materials by the Government would also allow such content to be incorporated or compiled into an existing publication.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Copying it, whether a part of it or the entirety of the materials is allowed if done for the permitted purposes and the permitted use does not prevent any parts that are copied from being combined along with other materials.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On fair use, Mr Don Wee, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Ms He Ting Ru had some questions on the changes that we have made to fair use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The question that has been asked is whether fair use has been reworked into an open-ended exception that requires the Courts to make a determination on a case-by-case basis and whether, with the fifth factor removed, the point that Mr Wee specifically bought up, we are now providing less guidance to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because of the language and because of the way in which it was framed, users had assumed, in many cases, wrongly, that they first had to procure a licence before they could get within the rubric of the fifth factor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members would also know that clause 191 requires the Court to consider "all relevant matters" in deciding whether a work or a performance is fairly used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the removal of the fifth factor simply means that the Court only needs to consider that factor when it is of the view that that factor is relevant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What the current Bill does is it provides for the four factors, the Court considers all four factors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in the appropriate case or in such cases which are particularly fact-sensitive, the Courts can still consider this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in fact, this is what the Chief Justice said in a leading Court of Appeal decision in Global Yellow Pages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court of Appeal, without taking Members through the decision in detail, opined that looking at fair dealing as it currently is called, is overall highly fact-sensitive inquiry that has to have regard to all the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All the factors must be considered but the Court, of course, understands the facts, ascertains the context, looks at the parties' relative position and then, assigns the appropriate weight to each factor and makes an overall determination whether a dealing is fair or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, this approach will continue and the Court will have regard to each case, looking at the facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think if you look at the construct of the fair use exceptions, this is precisely what it is intended to do – to allow the Courts, the adjudicators to look at the specific factual matrix behind each contention for exception or for use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me touch on the CMOs which several Members spoke about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked whether the Government would be regulating the amount of royalties to be paid to CMOs and what recourse users have if the amount is unreasonable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Shawn Huang asked how the regulations could affect foreign CMOs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas suggested that CMOs may need more time to adapt to the regulations and it should not be too onerous as to be prohibitive to new entrants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Copyright Tribunal will continue to hear disputes over reasonableness of licence fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That was the case and will still be the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also mentioned the timeline for these regulations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will give CMOs more time to make the necessary adjustments to regulation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are mindful that the CMOs might need the extra time and we are continuously engaging with them and have done so since our CMO public consultations started a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I can assure Mr Thomas that the scheme will be a light-touch class licensing regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we similarly want to encourage new entrants in this area with innovative solutions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Regulations, as some Members have pointed out, will provide clarity to all, but at the same time, we do not intend to make it burdensome to CMOs who operate in a responsible and accountable manner.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To achieve the right balance in our regulations, we have considered the experience of other countries and international precedents in WIPO's Good Practice Toolkit for CMOs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The term simply means that the user is permitted to do an act under the law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 183 explains that an act that is a permitted use is not a rights infringement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will help to prevent misunderstandings about the use of that term.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling suggested that persons with intellectual disabilities and audio disabilities could have similar levels of permitted uses as persons with print disabilities and also that permitted uses should all be made mandatory.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether there could be a one-stop publishing house dealing with all the IP rights.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling spoke about models that need to have some form of protection as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim spoke about permitted use for publicly-funded research, which I believe I responded to earlier in the context of fair use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas suggested that we consider legislation that can determine the ownership of AI-generated works.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Ms He Ting Ru had a suggestion on mandating royalties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are all suggestions that are not covered in this Bill but we will study them and decide at the appropriate stage whether they can be implemented or they can be implemented with modifications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want to tell Members of this House that our review of the copyright regime does not stop with the passing of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continually review, particularly given that we are dealing with an industry sector that is very fast changing and fast moving, and will take on board suggestions as they come in for our continual review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Wee had a suggestion that went beyond this framework, on whether there could be a valuation and financing framework for collateralising copyright.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I recently spoke at the launch of the Singapore IP Strategy 2030 during this year's IP Week @ SG event, outlining the efforts on valuation of IP.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore will be involved with an international valuation panel to develop valuation guidelines for intangible assets and IP.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The guidelines will be based on internationally accepted standards that can be then widely adopted internationally and they will help rights owners commercialise and maximise the value of their IP, including through collateralisation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay had various suggestions for freelancers and the general public.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Mr Lim Biow Chuan urged that there must be public education on the change in the default ownership rules for certain commissioned works.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think Members were particularly taken with the point about photography and wedding photographs, in particular.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was an example that came up with more than once.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip asked what the Government would be doing to build up a culture of acknowledging sources and identifying creators in our schools, given the new permitted use of freely available materials from the Internet for educational purposes which requires acknowledgment of the source as a condition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, we will be reaching out to the various stakeholders to help them understand their new rights and will also be working with them to make sure that the broader public is kept informed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, we will work with the National Arts Council and NTUC to educate creators and performers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will work closely with MOE to ensure that teachers and students are aware of the details of the new permitted use.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For changes which affect a broad spectrum of stakeholders, like the changes in default ownership of commissioned works or the new right to be identified, we will reach out through various channels, infographics, social media and public talks, to make sure that information is disseminated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members can avail themselves of online resources and bring them to the attention of members in their constituencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked what we do with Parmesan cheese and whiskey.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Assoc Prof Lim might know that this is not within the purview of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When Ms He Ting Ru closed her speech, she mentioned clauses 141 and 142 on penalties, but then quickly segued into talking about the cost of foreign sports programmes being broadcast on TV.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Ms He knows that this is also not relevant to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the result of exclusivity of negotiated broadcast, licences and rights, and it is not an issue that this Bill can fix.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, the point here is you cannot remove copyright.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You cannot take away the copyright because, quite frankly, if you do, then the content will simply not come into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is quite a different debate altogether that Ms He has raised on this issue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not germane to this Bill and I would not say anything beyond this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We continue to chart a path that is both fair and reasonable to both sides of the equation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We do this in the context of the technological and the market changes that are constantly occurring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had addressed in my opening speech the reasons for making the amendments to clause 247.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had also addressed the reasons for making this amendment in my opening speech.
